analysis.one_liner: Taxes polluting industries to fund clean water projects and help low-income households afford water bills.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995; it had one sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have kept $2 billion a year in federal clean water aid and added another $4 billion a year from new taxes on the things that pollute water: chemical discharges into waterways and sewage plants, fertilizer and pesticides, and water sold for commercial and industrial use. The money would flow through state revolving loan funds to sewage treatment plants, pollution runoff control, and new grant programs for towns of 5,000 people or fewer and communities where water bills are eating up family income. It would also require affordable water and sewer rates for households near or below the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households in areas where water and sewer bills exceed a set share of income would be guaranteed affordable rates through a new assurance program [S3]. Small towns of 5,000 or fewer and 'hardship' communities could get grants instead of loans [S3]. States would get expanded funding for sewage plants, watershed management, and nonpoint pollution control, with at least 15 percent of federal grants reserved for runoff control [S3]. Taxpayers generally benefit because the bill's findings set a goal of shifting most of the cost onto polluters rather than the general fund [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a low-income water and sewer assurance program requiring that water and sewer rates not exceed roughly 4 percent of gross monthly income for households at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level, with benefits counted as non-income for tax and benefit purposes [S3].

Authorizes state revolving funds to make grants for small communities (5,000 people or fewer), hardship communities where combined water and sewer bills exceed 2 percent of median family income, nonpoint pollution control, and low-income rate assistance [S3].

Provides $2 billion a year from the general fund plus $4 billion a year from a new Clean Water Trust Fund financed entirely by pollution-related excise taxes, toward an estimated national need the bill's findings put at more than $200 billion over 20 years [S3].

Extends the maximum loan term from 20 years to the expected life of the financed facility and reserves at least 15 percent of each state's capitalization grant for nonpoint source pollution control, such as agricultural runoff [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities discharging listed chemical pollutants would pay per-pound excise taxes ranging from fractions of a cent to over $60 a pound depending on toxicity [S3]. Fertilizer, pesticide, and processed animal feed manufacturers and importers would pay new excise taxes on nitrogen, phosphorus, active ingredients, and feed tonnage [S3]. Commercial and industrial water users would pay 1.95 cents per thousand gallons; residential, farm, hydroelectric, and government uses are exempt [S3]. Some of these costs would be passed to consumers through prices of chemicals, food, and industrial goods.

drawbacks.text: The fertilizer, pesticide, and feed taxes would raise input costs for American farmers, who are exempt from the discharge and water-use taxes but not from these upstream taxes; exports are exempt but domestic use is not [S3].

The 1.95-cent-per-thousand-gallon tax on commercial and industrial water use would be collected by utilities from the users and would likely be passed through to consumers in the prices of manufactured goods and services [S3].

The per-pound discharge tax covers a very long list of pollutants in five groups with rates from 0.6 cents to $63.39 per pound, creating substantial measurement, reporting, and compliance burdens for dischargers [S3].
Ordinary taxpayers would continue paying $2 billion a year from the general fund in addition to the industry taxes, which the bill itself frames as the taxpayer's 'fair share' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households and small towns the bill targets, the benefits are direct and substantial: grant aid for small and hardship communities, longer loan terms, and a guaranteed affordability standard for low-income ratepayers. The costs fall on chemical, fertilizer, and pesticide manufacturers and industrial water users, and some of that cost would reach ordinary consumers through higher prices for chemicals, food, and manufactured goods. The bill's design deliberately shifts the biggest share of clean water funding from general taxpayers onto polluting activities, which is a defensible trade-off, but the complexity of taxing hundreds of listed pollutants per pound would have been a real administrative challenge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sat in a Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittee, was pointed to a later similar bill (H.R. 3948) in March 1994, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Norman Mineta introduced the bill on May 25, 1993, and it was referred to both the Public Works and Transportation Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the committee with jurisdiction over taxes [S1], [S5].
On June 7, 1993, it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee; no further action was recorded on the bill itself [S5].

On March 3, 1994, the action history notes 'See H.R. 3948', indicating similar legislation became the vehicle for the effort, and H.R. 2255 itself received no vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5], [S1].
The bill had a single sponsor and zero cosponsors throughout its life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that would have paid the new taxes — chemical manufacturers discharging listed pollutants, fertilizer and pesticide makers, and commercial and industrial water users — avoided an estimated $4 billion a year in excise taxes. Low-income ratepayers and small-town utilities gained nothing and continued to bear rising water and sewer costs, and taxpayers continued to carry the federal share without a polluter-based funding stream.

for.name: Rep. Norman Mineta
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor; no colleague joined as a cosponsor [S5], [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Tax-writing committee with jurisdiction over the bill's excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and recorded no action on the bill during the entire Congress, leaving its Title II tax provisions unconsidered [S5].

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Primary committee of jurisdiction over the Clean Water Act
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat without a markup or hearing before the bill was superseded by H.R. 3948 [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor signed on, so no partisan split on the merits appears anywhere in the record [S4], [S5].

industries.note: The bill would tax discharges of hundreds of listed chemical pollutants into waterways and sewage treatment plants, from 0.6 cents to $63.39 per pound by toxicity group. The bill died, so these industries avoided the tax while the public continued bearing clean water costs through water bills and general taxes [S3].

industries.industry: Fertilizer, pesticide, and animal feed manufacturers
industries.note: New excise taxes on fertilizer nitrogen and phosphorus (0.845 cents/pound), pesticide active ingredients (24.27 cents/pound), and processed feed (2.68 cents/ton) would have targeted major sources of agricultural runoff pollution. These costs would partly reach consumers through food prices [S3].

A 1.95-cent-per-thousand-gallon tax on nonresidential water use, collected by utilities, would fall on businesses while residential, farm, and government users are exempt; business costs would be passed to consumers [S3].

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction and municipal utilities
industries.note: An additional $4 billion a year flowing through state revolving funds for treatment plants, watershed projects, and conservation would have expanded construction work and utility upgrades in communities that currently cannot afford them [S3].
